item.title: Portable Extended-Precision Floating-Point Arithmetic for Scientific Computing Kernels
item.description: arXiv:2611.28959v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many scientific computations need more accuracy than IEEE double precision, but arbitrary precision is often too costly on CPUs and GPUs. Multi-float arithmetic fills this gap by representing each value as an unevaluated sum of IEEE numbers. Existing implementations are generally confined to a CPU, CUDA, or language-specific programming model. We present MultiFloats.cpp, a header-only C++17 library that uses Kokkos to compile the same extended-precision kernels for Serial, OpenMP, CUDA, and HIP. The library supports Float64x2 through Float64x4 (106--212 bits) and the corresponding Float32-based types. We evaluate it using seven SHOC-style kernels and compare against QD, CAMPARY, MPFR, and Julia MultiFloats.jl on A100, GH200, and AMD RX 780M systems. On A100, Float64x4 addition sustains 15,700 MOps/s, or 1.5 times CAMPARY; on CPU, vectorized Float64x4 operations are 4.2--6.6 times faster than QD's qd_real. Addition and multiplication produce 0 ULP error over 10,000 inputs, while Float64x4 division and square root remain within 1.71 and 17.9 ULP, respectively. Thus, extended precision can remain practical and portable without separate backend implementations.
item.dc:creator: Manas Vishal

item.title: Computing $ab+cd$ and other expressions with correct rounding in binary floating-point arithmetic
item.description: arXiv:2611.30415v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce two ``high-level'' algorithms that make it possible to evaluate the sum $(x\_h+x\_\ell) + (y\_h+y\_\ell)$ of two double-word numbers with correct rounding in binary floating-point arithmetic. These algorithms allow one to evaluate expressions of the form $ab+cd$, $a+b+cd$, $a+b+c+d$, and $abc$ with correct rounding, where $a$, $b$, $c$, and $d$ are floating-point numbers.
item.dc:creator: Stef Graillat (PASCALINE), Jean-Michel Muller (PASCALINE), Takeshi Ogita

item.title: Accurate Products, Inaccurate Inverse: Emulated FP64 BLAS in Blocked Triangular Inversion
item.description: arXiv:2611.31030v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: FP64 emulation on integer tensor units now ships in cuBLAS and GEMMul8, and each emulated matrix product can be checked against an accuracy grade. We ask if a routine built from such products inherits their accuracy, and show that blocked triangular inversion, the core of LAPACK's inverse of a symmetric positive definite matrix, does not. Under fixed-precision emulation every product passes the grade-B error bound of Demmel et al., yet the inverse errs at 7.1e-2, against 2.0e-15 natively. The matrices are well conditioned after diagonal scaling, but the scaling spans 64 binades. The cause is one product, T = X22 L21, whose summed index carries both the diagonal scaling and its inverse, which a grade-B bound does not absorb. Computing those products natively restores native accuracy; leaving any one of them emulated does not. The pattern holds on four GPUs, and on real covariance matrices the fixed-precision routes lose up to about four orders of accuracy. Equilibration, a solve-based association and cuBLAS's automatic dynamic precision avoid the loss, and an exact error recurrence audits a completed run. On an RTX 4090 the fastest accurate emulated inversion takes 0.40 of cuSOLVER's time. Where each product's scaling falls decides if per-product accuracy carries over to a composite routine, and that is what builders of emulated libraries need to check.
item.dc:creator: Erzheng Zhang

item.title: graspit-py: A Python Interface to GraspIt! for Grasp Planning Under Pose and Friction Uncertainty
item.description: arXiv:2611.29011v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In simulated multifingered grasps, pose error can change contacts formed during hand closure, while friction uncertainty changes the loads supported by those contacts. Existing C++ APIs and ROS 1 services provide programmatic GraspIt! access but require native bindings or a service transport layer for Python use and application-specific integration of contact geometry with uncertainty sampling. A Python workflow for these studies must connect native closure and contacts to caller-defined wrench scores, uncertainty samples, and command reconstruction. We present graspit-py, a Python interface to native GraspIt! operations that supplies this workflow. The interface provides native scene access, contact-wrench analysis, and configurable approach planning under pose and friction uncertainty. A grasp record associates the object-relative palm pose and closed independent coordinates with nominal contacts and quality scores evaluated under sampled pose and friction conditions. Our MuJoCo exporter derives serial hinge chains and affine joint couplings, including nonzero reference angles, and preserves individual collision components. Across 75 configurations of five hand models, maximum discrepancy between source and exported palm-frame vertex sets was approximately 1.3 micrometers against a 100-micrometer geometry tolerance. We isolated reference-angle and collision-component effects through controlled ablations and validated 1,920 directional task-wrench capacity calculations against independent Cartesian-force linear programs. In a common GraspIt! workload, median reset-close-score-state cycle latency through direct Python was 10.7% lower than through persistent ROS 1 services. An executable export-plan-reconstruct workflow and grasp examples on six hand models demonstrate how the contact, score, and joint representations support numerical analysis and command reconstruction.
item.dc:creator: Clinton Enwerem, John S. Baras, Calin Belta

item.title: Ziv: A Language for Correctly Rounded Math Libraries
item.description: arXiv:2611.30346v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Developing performant, correctly rounded math libraries is challenging. Such implementations often rely on extended-precision arithmetic for correct rounding and precomputed constants for performance. Existing implementation languages, however, provide limited support for (i) high-level abstractions for such arithmetic and (ii) staged computation to combine precomputation and runtime computation in one program. As a result, existing implementations often miss abstraction opportunities and hard-code constants precomputed using separate programs. These practices make it difficult to write, understand, and modify these libraries. We present Ziv, a programming system for developing correctly rounded math libraries. It consists of a small language, a rich standard library, and a provably sound compiler targeting C. Ziv supports (i) high-level numerical abstractions via types and operations for extended-precision numbers, and (ii) staged computation via compile-time evaluation of expressions known to be input-independent. These features enable high-level code that unifies precomputation and runtime computation. We embed Ziv in Julia and evaluate it by reimplementing 19 functions from two state-of-the-art libraries targeting correct rounding; we achieve competitive performance with 2.63$\times$ reductions in lines of code. We also implement three new functions and automatically explore 824,256 variants, achieving 96.5$\times$ average speedup over an arbitrary-precision library.
item.dc:creator: Lucas Yunkyu Lee, Sungjin Hwang, Wonyeol Lee

item.title: AI-Assisted Auto-formalization for Trustworthy Scientific Computing: Case Studies and Lessons Learned
item.description: arXiv:2611.31033v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Agentic AI tools have recently had success in mathematical reasoning. Both general purpose coding agents such as Claude Code and Codex, and specialized mathematics agents such as Aristotle, have been used for formalizing mathematical problems such as Fermat's last theorem, Erd\H{o}s problems and several IMO level math problems. However, much of these efforts are concentrated in the pure mathematics domain, which benefits from relatively self-contained theorem statements, fixed mathematical representation and extensive support in existing formal libraries. Applied mathematics, on the other hand, presents additional challenges because the source may describe a computational procedure or modeling transformation rather than a declarative theorem. In this work, we present a systematic study of AI-assisted auto-formalization for scientific computing (SC), a domain in applied mathematics central to U.S. Department of Energy applications. Through case studies spanning hierarchical abstraction layers in SC software stack, we evaluate not only whether AI agents can complete numerical proofs, but also where and why they fail across the stack. Our primary contribution is a cross-layer taxonomy of failure modes and an analysis of the form of expert feedback required at each layer to recover mathematical soundness. From these observations, we derive a workflow for recurring proof patterns and practical guidance for using AI agents while preserving mathematical soundness. Our results characterize both the practical value and the current limitations of AI-assisted formalization for trustworthy scientific computing.
item.dc:creator: Mohit Tekriwal, Het Mankad, Naifeng Zhang, Keita Teranishi, Sahil Bhola, Daisuke Uchida, Jean-Baptiste Jeannin, Franz Franchetti, Karthik Duraisamy, Jeffrey Vetter, Yohann Dudouit

item.title: Native Rectangular Linear Assignment with Implicit Rejection: A Jonker-Volgenant Solver without Square Expansion
item.description: arXiv:2610.35948v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Rectangular assignment with a uniform unmatched penalty is often implemented by expanding the cost matrix. We integrate established rectangular Jonker-Volgenant principles and implicit rejection with float64 working arithmetic and reusable workspaces in Rust (JVRUST), hybrid Rust/C++ (JVHYBRID) and C++ (JVCPP). A campaign evaluates laprust/lapcpp 1.2.0 and LAPX 0.13.0 in four Windows/Linux and Python environments. Each environment contains 302 cases: 3,286 complete-call timing conditions with five inputs and three rounds, plus 91 memory conditions with five fresh-process trials. Against the matching compact SciPy reference, all three native implementations exceed a 3% advantage on all 102 required cases; JVRUST and JVCPP do so on 163-165 and 163-166 of 166 optional cases, respectively. Controlled comparisons qualify these gains by representation, initialization, sparsity, batching and orientation. We also assess how solver gains carry over to pedestrian and cell tracking using real-world data and prepared detections. In each Windows environment, the specialized LSAPE code wins 38 of 67 cases against the original Hungarian implementation and all 67 against its unchanged one-sided baseline. The contribution is software integration and reproducible performance characterization. Adverse results are retained; no algorithmic priority, statistical significance or universal solver ranking is claimed. The initialization policy was developed using related workload families, so the campaign is not a held-out test of heuristic optimality.
item.dc:creator: Ratha Siv, Raphael Reme, Matei Mancas, Bernard Gosselin
